content_list.content_text: Film noir is hard to define. Is it a genre, a style, a mood or a look? Does a noir film have to be shot in black and white? Does it need to be set in a city? Must it involve a violent crime? Does the ending have to be unhappy? Were true noir films produced only in the United States during a classic period, from 1941 to 1958? Should films produced elsewhere or after that period be classified as neo-noir, retro-noir or even as a cheap copy of noir films?

information.contentText: The cinematographer of The Big Combo (1955) was John Alton (1901-1996), also known for T-Men (1947) and Raw Deal (1948). With his work, the iconic cameraman laid the foundation for the atmosphere of noir films.

content_list.content_text: Film historians have debated these issues for years without ever reaching a consensus. Some have broadened the definition of film noir even further. The ever-controversial British critic Raymond Durgnat included King Kong (1933) and 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) in his noir pantheon, which perhaps diluted the concept beyond all reason. But most critics accept that noir Westerns (Pursued, 1947), noir costume dramas (Reign of Terror, 1949) and even some British noir films (Night and the City, 1950 - the quintessential noir title) can legitimately be included in the canon.

quote.quote: People lose teeth talking like that. If you want to hang around, you'll be polite.
quote.author: Humphrey Bogart (Sam Spade) in The Maltese Falcon (1941)

content_list.content_text: Deciding when Hollywood film noir began is also a problem. Its origins go back to the shadows, angles and paranoid world of German Expressionism, and refugees from Nazism such as Fritz Lang (1890-1976), Robert Siodmak (1900-1973) and Karl Freund (1890-1969) certainly brought with them visual and thematic elements that fed into conventional Hollywood films and made them darker.

This generation of European filmmakers understood cinema's potential for creating complex psychological effects while exploring controversial themes - something already present in the work of directors such as Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980), who made his first film noir, Shadow of a Doubt (1943). Fritz Lang's (1890-1976) M - Eine Stadt sucht einen Mörder (M, 1931), about a serial child killer, is one of the first crime films to combine the dark look and the typical plot of film noir.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Out of the Past (1947)
information.contentText: Out of the Past (1947), directed by Jacques Tourneur (1904-1977), displays many of the hallmarks of noir films: a cynical private detective as the protagonist, a femme fatale, several flashbacks with voice-over narration, dramatically shadowed cinematography and a fatalistic humor leavened with provocative wisecracks.

content_list.content_text: The German thriller featured the quintessential noir actor, Peter Lorre (1904-1964), in an incredibly frightening performance; it also had voice-over narration, a device that would become one of the genre's trademarks. Another Lang film, You Only Live Once (1937), with a doomed young couple (Henry Fonda and Sylvia Sidney) fleeing fate and the law, also seems to anticipate aspects of film noir. Even so, neither of these two works conveys the sense of existential claustrophobia and mysterious duplicity that characterizes the typical noir film.

content_list.title: Etymology
content_list.description: The term was first applied to a film by French critic Nino Frank in 1946, by analogy with the crime novels of the Série noire, a collection created by Gallimard in 1945, whose books had black and yellow covers, with a black dust jacket and white borders. The term was unknown to directors and actors at the time the classic noir films were made, having been introduced later by film historians and critics. Many of the creators of films noirs later revealed that they had no idea, at the time, that they had given rise to a film subgenre. Noir derives from the suspense novels of the Great Depression era (many were adapted from crime novels of the period) and from the aesthetics of 1930s horror films. The first noirs appeared in the early 1940s. Historically, they were shot in high-contrast black and white, under the influence of German Expressionist cinematography.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text published on "Wikipedia"

content_list.content_text: Another film sometimes considered Hollywood's first noir production is Stranger on the Third Floor (1940), a complex and dark thriller, also starring European expatriate Peter Lorre. But it was just a 64-minute B movie directed by the unknown Boris Ingster (1903-1978). Despite the cinematography of Nicholas Musuraca, one of the finest cinematographers of film noir, it had little influence at the time. The film most often championed as the one that kicked off the noir cycle in Hollywood is the crime film The Maltese Falcon (1941), even though its producers had no intention of starting a trend, much less of launching one of the most analyzed, admired and influential cycles in film history.

information.contentText: The unusual lighter that adorns Sam Spade's (Humphrey Bogart) desk is a Ronson Touch-Tip table model. Manufactured by Ronson Co. from 1935 to 1951, it is a classic example of the "art deco" style that dominated that era. The originals are so sought after by collectors that there is now at least one company devoted entirely to restoring original examples.

content_list.content_text: The elusiveness of the genre may have been caused, in part, by the fact that it was only called noir after the fact. The concept is a retrospective historical creation, similar to expressions such as "Middle Ages". Filmmakers who made Westerns, tough-guy films or biopics knew exactly what rules they were working with; few (if any) directors of noir films would have referred to their productions as a distinct genre.

The heroes of film noir are rarely nice guys. Cynical, ruthless, always looking for an angle and utterly unsentimental, they were typically lonely, insecure and disillusioned men, unsure of their own character and apathetic about the future. They were generally played by actors such as Humphrey Bogart and Robert Mitchum - star of the seminal work of film noir, Out of the Past (1947) - who were able to get the most out of their characters on screen.

information.contentText: Adapted by director Billy Wilder and writer Raymond Chandler from the crime novel by James M. Cain, Double Indemnity is the archetypal noir film, the story of a desperate woman and a greedy man, of a murder for dirty money and of a sudden, violent betrayal. Even so, it has a strange and provocative romanticism ("How could I have known that murder could sometimes smell like honeysuckle?") and ends, remarkably for 1944, with a confession not only of murder but also of love between two men. The last line, spoken by the dying Fred MacMurray to the inconsolable Edward G. Robinson, is: "I love you, too".

content_list.content_text: In the world of noir, even if the hero is lucky enough to survive to the end of the story, he rarely gets the girl. The genre is characterized by a lack of trust between characters, by a loss of innocence, by a hostile urban setting (as in Cry of the City, 1948) and by a sense of despair - usually offset by a biting humor that keeps the audience on the verge of depression. Noir served as a reaction to the Hollywood musicals and romantic comedies of the time. While mainstream cinema prided itself on its spotless heroes and sugary heroines, film noir showcased a platoon of antiheroes and femmes fatales.

quote.quote: Since Double Indemnity, the two most important words in motion pictures are 'Billy' and 'Wilder'
quote.author: Alfred Hitchcock

content_list.content_text: The classic period of Hollywood film noir coincides with the years of World War II and the postwar anti-communist witch hunt. Noir films, with their intimidating atmosphere of fear and paranoia and their sense of fatalism, served as an indirect reaction to the political climate of the time. In many of them, one can detect a certain anxiety about the conflict ravaging Europe that would eventually draw in the United States - or, years later, about the claustrophobic climate of the Cold War, which stifled the whole country, as did the threat of nuclear annihilation.

John Huston (1906-1987) directed The Maltese Falcon before the United States entered the war; even so, it is possible to sense, hidden beneath the traditional portrayal of the private detective, a certain apprehension about events in Europe. The Third Man (1949), directed by Carol Reed (1906-1976) and set and shot in postwar Vienna, delves into the chaos that followed World War II and reflects the prevailing atmosphere of anxiety, pessimism and uncertainty.

information.contentText: A rare British film that is technically as perfect as the best Hollywood classics - Reed would never make anything so masterful again - The Third Man is an extraordinary blend of political thriller, strange love story, gothic mystery and black-and-white romantic torment. Welles, who is truly brilliant in the five minutes he is on screen, got all the attention, but this is a film of impeccable performances, with wonderful work from Cotten as the dazed, disappointed hero and the radiant beauty of Italian star Valli as the pro forma heroine. This is a film that glows throughout, with its nighttime cityscapes, its anguished faces and the rushing waters of the sewers in the finale.

content_list.content_text: Occupied Vienna is controlled by four different military powers, while a murky black market in drugs plagues the already devastated city. Urban landscapes often served as the setting for this kind of film. The dark, damp streets of the big cities created the perfect backdrop for the terrifying events and uneasy atmosphere of film noir. Among the favorite techniques of film noir are low-key chiaroscuro lighting, odd angles, flashbacks, first-person voice-over narration, fast and biting dialogue, and nonlinear narratives. The cinematographers of the time, among them Nicholas Musuraca (1892-1975), John F. Seitz (1892-1979) and John Alton (1901-1996), used expressionist lighting to create the ideal atmosphere and emphasize tension. Arthur Edeson (1891-1970) is considered the creator of classic noir cinematography.

He shot his first film in 1914 and went on to film several of Douglas Fairbanks's swashbucklers and one of the first sound films, All Quiet on the Western Front (1930). Also in the 1930s, Edeson was responsible for the cinematography of some classic Universal horror films directed by James Whale (1889-1957): Frankenstein (1931), The Old Dark House (1932) and The Invisible Man (1933), in which the combination of German Expressionism with a dark gothic atmosphere and overblown melodrama served to set the standard for horror films. In 1941 he worked as cinematographer on The Maltese Falcon.

information.contentText: The film The Blue Dahlia was based on a novel by Raymond Chandler. It stars Alan Ladd and Veronica Lake, a famous film noir couple.

content_list.content_text: The plots and themes of film noir are rooted in the cheap pulp magazines and American crime novels of the time, whose tone was transferred to the dialogue of the screenplays. Double Indemnity (1944), another noir classic, was adapted by director Billy Wilder (1906-2002) and writer Raymond Chandler from a novel by James M. Cain. Chandler's writing inspired several important noir films, among them The Big Sleep (1946).

During the 1940s and 1950s, the tone of film noir grew even more intense. The dark areas became more melancholy and transgressive; the lights, bolder and more hysterical; and the framing, more vertiginous, while the sense of fatalism intensified and became even more internalized. "Fate, or some mysterious force," reflects the hero of Detour (1945), "can put the finger on you or me for no good reason at all".

Other traumas of the period darkened the picture: anti-communist paranoia, postwar disorientation and a sense of emptiness. Crossfire (1947) points to the violent potential of war veterans; the specter of Nazism is present in Notorious (1946); a nagging worry about wives and girlfriends falling prey to interlopers on the home front runs through The Blue Dahlia (1946); and alcoholism, a growing problem in postwar America, nearly destroys the hero of The Lost Weekend (1945).

information.contentText: One of the greatest B movies ever made, Detour does not try to reach beyond its tight budget and shooting schedule. Instead, it makes the most of its own simplicity, presenting a world somewhere between pulp fiction and existentialism, in which life has low production values and a short running time.

content_list.content_text: Orson Welles's (1915-1985) audacious Touch of Evil (1958) marked the end of the American cycle of film noir. The film became famous for its uninterrupted three-minute opening take, for its final chase scene, with its extravagant visuals and experimental sound effects.

As the United States sank into Cold War neurosis, the gloomy, fatalistic vision of film noir seemed like a response to, and a disenchanted expression of, the optimism and patriotism found in most Hollywood productions. Those patriotic parades on the avenues of major cities had a bitter flip side in the mean streets: the brighter the spotlights and the louder the drums, the darker the shadows and the greater the emptiness the films echoed.

As film historian Colin McArthur put it: "The themes of film noir are not social; they do not refer to the problems (...) of a specific society; they are metaphysical and have to do with anguish and loneliness, which are essential elements of the human condition."

information.contentText: The famous long-take chase scene in Touch of Evil (1958), a fitting end to the American cycle of film noir.

movies.title: The Maltese Falcon
movies.overview: A private detective takes on a case that involves him with three eccentric criminals, a beautiful liar, and their quest for a priceless statuette.

movies.title: Double Indemnity
movies.overview: A rich woman and a calculating insurance agent plot to kill her unsuspecting husband after he signs a double indemnity policy. Against a backdrop of distinctly Californian settings, the partners in crime plan the perfect murder to collect the insurance, which pays double if the death is accidental.

movies.title: The Third Man
movies.overview: In postwar Vienna, Austria, Holly Martins, a writer of pulp Westerns, arrives penniless as a guest of his childhood chum Harry Lime, only to learn he has died. Martins develops a conspiracy theory after learning of a "third man" present at the time of Harry's death, running into interference from British officer Major Calloway, and falling head-over-heels for Harry's grief-stricken lover, Anna.

movies.title: Shadow of a Doubt
movies.overview: A bored teen living in Santa Rosa, California, Charlotte "Charlie" Newton, is frustrated because nothing seems to be happening in her life and that of her family. Then, she receives wonderful news: her uncle (for whom she was named), Charlie Oakley, is arriving for a visit. But Uncle Charlie may not be the man he seems to be.

movies.title: Casablanca
movies.overview: In Casablanca, Morocco in December 1941, a cynical American expatriate meets a former lover, with unforeseen complications.

movies.title: The Big Sleep
movies.overview: Private Investigator Philip Marlowe is hired by wealthy General Sternwood regarding a matter involving his youngest daughter Carmen. Before the complex case is over, Marlowe sees murder, blackmail, deception, and what might be love.

movies.title: The Blue Dahlia
movies.overview: Soon after a veteran's return from war his cheating wife is found dead. He evades police in an attempt to find the real murderer.

movies.title: The Postman Always Rings Twice
movies.overview: A married woman and a drifter fall in love, then plot to murder her husband.

movies.title: Dead Reckoning
movies.overview: Paratroopers Captain 'Rip' Murdock  and Sergeant Johnny Drake are mysteriously ordered to travel to Washington, DC. When Drake learns that he is to be awarded the Medal of Honor, he disappears before newspaper photographers can take his picture. Murdock follows the clues and tracks him down, where he learns Drake is dead. Further investigations reveal unexpected twists. Rip learns that Johnny had been accused of murder and sets out to find out whatever he can. He falls in love with Coral whose husband Johnny is supposed to have killed.

movies.title: Out of the Past
movies.overview: Jeff Bailey seems to be a mundane gas station owner in remote Bridgeport, CA. He is dating local girl Ann Miller and lives a quiet life. But Jeff has a secret past, and when a mysterious stranger arrives in town, Jeff is forced to return to the dark world he had tried to escape.

movies.title: Touch of Evil
movies.overview: When a car bomb explodes on the American side of the U.S./Mexico border, Mexican drug enforcement agent Miguel Vargas begins his investigation, along with American police captain Hank Quinlan. When Vargas begins to suspect that Quinlan and his shady partner, Menzies, are planting evidence to frame an innocent man, his investigations into their possible corruption quickly put himself and his new bride, Susie, in jeopardy.

content_list.description: Asian cinema gains even more prominence with the release of several masterpieces. Film noir emerges and musicals continue to shine on the big screen. The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
